items.title: Fake Job Offer Emails Are Installing Bad Programs — Don't Open the Attachment
items.summary: Scammers are sending fake job offer emails — notes about a "position" you never applied for, with a file attached. Opening that file quietly installs a bad program on your computer, and security researchers say this newest wave is already spreading. If a job offer shows up out of nowhere, don't open the attachment. Delete the message. Looking for work? Go straight to the company's website and apply there. Never click a link in an email that's trying to hand you a job you didn't ask for.

items.title: Type with your voice for free — Windows Voice Typing is built into Windows 11, press the Windows key + H
items.summary: Click into any text box, press the Windows key + H, and start talking — Windows Voice Typing types your words for you, free, with nothing to download. It's already on your Windows 11 computer; if nothing happens, check that the microphone is turned on at Settings > Privacy & security > Microphone.

items.title: Microsoft's August Windows update closes 400+ security holes — get it tonight at Settings > Windows Update
items.summary: Microsoft shipped its August 2026 Windows update on Tuesday and says to install it within days — it closes more than 400 security holes in Windows. Open Settings > Windows Update, click Check for updates, let it finish, and restart your computer once. Free, and it takes about ten minutes.

items.title: School's Back — So Are the Back-to-School Scams: Fake Laptop Deals and 'School' Emails
items.summary: School's back, and scammers are working the season. Crooks set up fake online stores advertising laptops at prices too good to be true — they take your money and card number, then vanish. Others send emails that look like they're from your child's school, asking you to log in or pay a fee. Real schools never do that. Type the store's web address yourself instead of clicking a link, and call the school using the number you already have if anything feels off.

items.title: Your computer forgets the time and date every morning? The tiny silver coin cell inside is worn out — about $2 at Walmart, CVS, or Amazon
items.summary: If your computer shows the wrong time and date every time you switch it on, the small round silver coin cell inside the case has run out of life. A fresh one costs about two dollars, and you can get it at Walmart, CVS, or Amazon — or a shop can put it in while you wait.

items.title: Google Chrome shipped a new security update on August 11 — see if yours has it in 30 seconds at chrome://settings/help
items.summary: Google pushed out a Chrome security update on Tuesday, August 11, 2026 that closes five security holes. Open Chrome, type chrome://settings/help in the address bar, and Chrome will grab it for free — then restart the browser and you are done.

items.title: Fake 'FCC' Callers Say Your Number Is Under Investigation — Hang Up
items.summary: Scammers are calling and texting people, pretending to be from the FCC — the government agency that watches over phones and the internet. According to the FCC, they say your phone number is under investigation for criminal activity and demand money or personal information to make it stop. That's a lie — no real agency does that. If you get this call, hang up. Don't call the number they give you, don't pay anything, and don't share personal information with anyone who calls out of the blue.

items.title: A Windows update is putting some computers on a "BitLocker recovery" screen — find your recovery key now, free, at account.microsoft.com/devices/recoverykey
items.summary: Microsoft's recent Windows updates have been sending some computers to a "BitLocker recovery" screen after they restart — that's the built-in lock that protects your files, and it asks for a 48-digit recovery key to prove the computer is yours. You can look yours up in about two minutes, before anything happens: sign in at `account.microsoft.com/devices/recoverykey` with the Microsoft account you use on that computer, and write the key down somewhere safe. If your machine was set up by an employer or a shop, ask whoever set it up.

items.title: Power flickers and your computer dies mid-work — a UPS keeps it running through outages, APC Back-UPS from about 60 dollars at apc.com
items.summary: A UPS — that's a power station your computer plugs into — keeps things running when the electricity blinks or goes out, long enough to save your work and turn the computer off the right way. APC Back-UPS is the one I recommend; find it at `apc.com`, or compare CyberPower at `cyberpowersystems.com`. You'll also see them at Best Buy and Office Depot. Get one big enough for your computer and monitor.

items.title: Fake CCleaner Download Pages Are Hiding Bad Programs — Check the Web Address First
items.summary: Scammers built a fake website that looks exactly like the download page for CCleaner, a popular free cleanup program. People who downloaded it got a bad program hiding on their computer that could watch everything they typed and steal passwords and bank logins. The same trick is spreading with fake copies of 7-Zip and Adobe programs. Only download software from the company's official website — check the web address at the very top of your screen first. If you're not sure, close the page and ask me.

items.title: ChatGPT now lets free users text as much as they want — no subscription needed, just sign up free at chatgpt.com
items.summary: OpenAI announced this week that free ChatGPT accounts can now send unlimited text messages — no paid plan required. Just open chatgpt.com on your computer, sign up for a free account, and start typing. Picture-making and file uploads still have their own limits, but everyday questions, email drafts, and homework help are wide open.

items.title: Log in to Windows with your fingerprint instead of a password — Windows Hello is built in and free at Settings > Accounts > Sign-in options
items.summary: Windows Hello is built into Windows and lets you sign in with your fingerprint — nothing to remember, and nobody can guess it. If your laptop has the little fingerprint square near the keyboard, set it up in about two minutes at Settings > Accounts > Sign-in options and choose "Fingerprint recognition." Microsoft just made the same sign-in work on desktop PCs with a plug-in fingerprint reader. It's free and already part of Windows.
